entries.title: Dear Abby: New living arrangement would come with serious strings
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> After four months of dating, I asked my boyfriend if we could move in together to save on rent. He was absolutely against the idea. We've now been dating for 10 months, and he recently got a letter stating that he's about to be evicted because he hasn't paid rent for three months. Now that he is about to lose his place, he says that because it's been 10 months of us dating, he should move in.</p><p>I have asked him for months to get a second job. He has a job that's based on commission only, so there are times he doesn't get paid unless he sells something. I have the same job but also work another one. He only recently applied to get another job, but he hasn't completed the requirements to fulfill the opening.</p><p>Do you think he is asking me to move in because he thinks I'll pay the bills? Also, his mom is living with him because she has memory problems. What should I do? This feels like a situation where I want to help but I don't want to be in a ruckus in the end. — <i>INDECISIVE IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR INDECISIVE:</b> You have known this man for only 10 months. That his moving in with you would also involve his mother who has memory problems creates an additional complication besides the fact that his income is so irregular he can't afford to pay his rent. What if his mother's problem worsens? Who will care for her while he's working? Will he be able to find a job for which he is qualified to supplement his income?</p><p>You are generous and caring, but if you do what he is asking, your relationship will become increasingly complicated, and a "ruckus" would be the least of your worries. He needs to solve his own problem without involving you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I don't like living where I am. I'm in a 55-plus community. I am 59, which is younger than a lot of people who live here. The gossiping here is awful and out of control. I was just informed by a neighbor that people who live here are afraid of me because of the way that I dress. I usually wear long jean shorts that reach my knees and a tucked-in T-shirt with a belt.</p><p>I have reached the point that I am having my dinner delivered, and I no longer go to breakfast in the dining room. I'm happier cooking my own food at home and keeping to myself. I am considering moving to a regular condo, not a 55-plus. At this point in my life, I need to be around younger people. Would you stay or would you move? — <i>UNCOMFORTABLE IN GEORGIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCOMFORTABLE:</b> Could some of your neighbors be jealous because you look so appealing in your "uniform"? Are you sure the person who told you that your neighbors are afraid of you was telling the truth? If you have been living in that 55-plus community only a short while, perhaps you should give it a little more time. However, if you feel a younger community would be more welcoming and stimulating, start looking around at what your options may be.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Abby shares more than 100 of her favorite recipes in two booklets: "Abby's Favorite Recipes" and "More Favorite Recipes by Dear Abby." entries.title: New transit law takes effect as CTA, Metra, Pace enter new era
entries.summary: <p>Goodbye, RTA. Hello, NITA.</p><p>The retirement of the Regional Transportation Authority began Monday as its board was granted new powers by the landmark Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act, which took effect.</p><p>The first act of the board — which will retain the RTA name until Sept. 1 when NITA board members are seated — was to buoy CTA, Metra and Pace with a quarter-percent sales tax increase for the Chicago area.</p><p>The RTA sales tax hike, which goes into effect Aug. 1, increases public transit funding by $200 million in 2026 and more than $500 million next year. It applies to the six-county area around Chicago.</p><p>The sales tax increase was a provision of the NITA legislation, which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/16/illinois-transit-bill-signed-pritzker" target="_blank" >passed last fall in Springfield</a> to bail out the CTA, Metra and Pace. The agencies were facing deep potential cuts to bus and rail service as federal COVID-19 pandemic grants ran dry and ridership remained low.</p><p>In all, the NITA law should raise $1.5 billion a year for public transit in Illinois, after additional funds are redirected from the state's gas sales tax.</p><p>The funds not only save the agencies from potential cuts but should enhance bus and rail service.</p><p>"With this funding, riders will immediately begin to see service improvements across the region," RTA Executive Director Leanne Redden said.</p><p>Among the changes:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-759dfc92-5dc3-11f1-b645-058a6ee8290a"><li>More frequent CTA buses. The agency is expanding service to <a class="Link" href="https://www.rtachicago.org/uploads/images/general/Communities/Service-Improvements-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >more than two dozen routes</a> with the new money.</li><li>More Metra trains. The Rock Island District has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/27/metra-train-rock-island-joliet" target="_blank" >added over a dozen weekly trains</a>, and Metra will explore extending the Electric line farther south.</li><li>More frequent Pace buses. More weekend service.</li></ul><p>The law also changes the transit agencies' power dynamics. For decades, the RTA oversaw the budgets of CTA, Metra and Pace, but had little power to coordinate service and projects between them.</p><p>Not anymore.</p><p>The NITA board will have the power to set fares, demand a universal ticket system and potentially create its own regional transit police force.</p><p>That won't be decided until after a safety task force, currently entrusted to the Cook County sheriff's office, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/01/15/cta-metra-pace-security-nita-law" target="_blank" >recommends how to alter</a> how police patrol the system.</p><p>Currently, only Metra has its own police department. The CTA is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/10/chicago-transit-authority-cta-crime-security-plan-fta" target="_blank" >patrolled</a> by Chicago police and Cook County sheriff's deputies.</p><p>The NITA law notable strips Chicago's mayor of control over the CTA. Before Monday, the mayor had the power to appoint the majority of CTA's board. Now, the mayor can only appoint two of its seven members.</p>

entries.title: 2 robbed at gunpoint in River North
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are seeking a white SUV involved in the armed robbery of two men early Monday in the River North neighborhood. </p><p>No one was inured during the attack. </p><p>Two men, 19 and 23, were in the 600 block of North Clark Street around 3:45 a.m. when a group of five to six individuals held them at gunpoint and demanded their property, Chicago police said. </p><p>Both men complied and the group fled east on Ontario Street in a white SUV, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Man and woman found dead in Bellwood home
entries.summary: <p>An emergency response to a west suburban Bellwood home led to the discovery of two dead adults early Monday,officials said. </p><p>A unidentified woman and man were pronounced dead at 2:10 a.m. and at 2:28 p.m., respectively, inside a small brick house in the 1000 block of 32nd Avenue, police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>They two were taken to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, Bellwood fire officials said. </p><p>Details on the circumstances of the incident were not immediately available. </p>
